tips.title: Two conditions for a reaction
tips.body: Particles must **collide**, and they must collide with **enough energy** — at least the **activation energy**. A collision without enough energy achieves nothing, which is why *they collide more often* is only half an explanation.

tips.title: Temperature is the one that does both
tips.body: **Concentration, pressure and surface area** increase only the **frequency** of collisions. **Temperature** increases the frequency **and** makes the collisions **more energetic**, so more of them exceed the activation energy. Give **both** for temperature and only the first for the others.

tips.title: A catalyst lowers the hump, not the ends
tips.body: On a reaction profile a catalyst **lowers the activation energy** — the hump gets smaller — while the **reactants and products stay at the same levels**. So the **overall energy change is unchanged**. A diagram that moves the ends has drawn a different reaction.

tips.title: Spot a catalyst by what is missing
tips.body: A catalyst **is not used up**, so it **does not appear in the chemical equation**. If a substance speeds up the reaction but is absent from the equation — and is still there at the end — it is a catalyst.

tips.title: Smaller pieces, bigger ratio
tips.body: Halving the side of a cube doubles its **surface area to volume ratio**: a 2 cm cube cut to 1 cm goes from **3 : 1** to **6 : 1**. The mass is unchanged, so the same total product forms — just **faster**, because more particles are exposed to collide.

why.matters:
Collision theory is what turns five separate rate factors into one idea. Particles can only react if they **collide**, and only if the collision carries enough energy — the **activation energy** — to get the reaction started.

Everything that speeds a reaction up does one of those two things, and temperature is the most powerful factor because it does both. Once you have the two conditions, you can explain a factor you have never been taught, which is what the exam is really asking for.

examples.title: Why flour explodes and a sack of it does not
examples.body:
A bag of flour will not catch light if you hold a match to it. The same flour thrown into the air as dust burns in a fraction of a second, which is why a mill is built to vent an explosion and why sawdust and custard powder are treated with the same respect.

Nothing about the chemistry changed. Cutting a solid finer does not alter how much there is, only how much of it is **surface**: one cubic centimetre has 6 cm² as a lump and 600 cm² as dust. A hundred times the surface is a hundred times as many places to collide.

props.caption: The same 1 cm³ of solid, cut finer. The volume never changes.

visual.alt: Three bars in proportion showing the surface area of one cubic centimetre of solid: six square centimetres as a single lump, sixty as one millimetre grains and six hundred as fine dust

examples.title: The fridge is a rate control
examples.body:
Food goes off because of chemical reactions, so slowing the reactions down keeps it. That is all a fridge is, and it is why the freezer works better still.

Cooling does **two** things at once, which is why temperature is the strongest factor there is. The particles move more slowly, so they collide **less often**; and far fewer of the collisions that do happen carry the **activation energy**. The second effect is the bigger one, and it is the half most answers leave out.

visual.alt: A table of a warm room, a fridge and a freezer, showing particles moving more slowly at each step and far fewer collisions carrying enough energy to react

examples.title: Why washing powder works at 30 °C
examples.body:
A stain is a chemical problem, and the old answer was a hot wash: heat the water until the reaction goes fast enough to finish in an hour.

A **catalyst** gets there another way. The enzymes in biological powder give the reaction a route with a **lower activation energy**, so a much larger share of the collisions already have enough to react — at 30 °C. The catalyst is not used up and is still in the powder at the end; what has changed is the size of the hump, not how hard the particles are pushing.

visual.alt: An energy level diagram of the catalysed reaction, with a low hump between the stain and the soluble pieces it is broken into, the activation energy the enzyme has lowered

steps.title: Collision theory
steps.body:
**Collision theory explains how various factors affect rates of reactions.**

> **Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.**

There are therefore **two** requirements, and both matter:

1. the particles must **collide**
2. the collision must have **enough energy**

**The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the activation energy.** A collision with less than that does nothing at all — the particles simply bounce apart.

**So there are two ways to make a reaction faster:**

- make collisions **more frequent**
- make a **greater proportion** of them energetic enough

**Almost every factor does the first.** Only **temperature** does both.

**That distinction is the spine of the whole topic.** An answer that explains a temperature increase by saying *the particles collide more often* has given half the reason and will usually score half the marks. The other half is that the particles **move faster**, so **more collisions have energy above the activation energy**.

steps.title: Explaining each factor
steps.body:
**Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, and the surface area of solid reactants increases the frequency of collisions and so increases the rate of reaction.**

**Concentration.** More particles in the same volume of solution, so they are **closer together** and **collide more often**.

**Pressure.** Squeezing a gas into a smaller volume puts more particles in that space, so again they are **closer together** and **collide more often**. This is the gas equivalent of concentration.

**Surface area.** Breaking a solid into smaller pieces **exposes more of it**, so more particles are **available to be collided with**. The **surface area to volume ratio** rises: halving a 2 cm cube to 1 cm takes it from **3 : 1** to **6 : 1**.

**Temperature is different**, and the spec says so explicitly:

> **Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic, and so increases the rate of reaction.**

Particles at a higher temperature have **more kinetic energy**, so they **move faster**. Moving faster means they **collide more often** — and it also means **more of those collisions have energy above the activation energy**. Both effects push the rate up, and the second is usually the larger.

**Simple proportionality.** The spec asks you to use simple ideas about proportionality here. Doubling the concentration roughly **doubles** the frequency of collisions and so roughly **doubles** the rate. It is not exact, but it is the reasoning a question about *twice as concentrated* is looking for.

steps.title: Catalysts
steps.body:
**Catalysts change the rate of chemical reactions but are not used up during the reaction.** They are still there, unchanged, when the reaction has finished.

**Different reactions need different catalysts.** There is no universal catalyst, and the spec says you do not need to know the names of any beyond those given in the subject content.

**Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems** — the same idea, in living cells.

**How a catalyst works:**

> **Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing a different pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy.**

**That wording is worth taking apart.** A catalyst does **not** give the particles more energy, and it does **not** make them collide more often. It offers an **alternative route** to the same products — one whose **activation energy is lower**. Because the barrier is lower, a **greater proportion of collisions** have enough energy to react, so the rate rises.

**On a reaction profile** this shows as a **smaller hump**. The **reactant and product levels are unchanged**, so:

- the **activation energy is lower**
- the **overall energy change is exactly the same**

**A catalyst cannot change how much energy a reaction releases or absorbs.** It changes only how easily the reaction gets started.

**How to identify a catalyst in a question.** It **speeds up the reaction**, it is **not used up**, and it **does not appear in the chemical equation**. That last point is the most useful, because it is a fact about the page in front of you rather than about the chemistry.

visuals.alt: A reaction profile for an exothermic reaction without a catalyst, showing a large activation energy hump between the reactants and the lower products level
A reaction profile for the same exothermic reaction with a catalyst, showing a smaller activation energy hump but the same reactant and product levels and the same overall energy change

steps.title: Explaining a rate change properly
steps.body:
**Almost every rate question is asking for a chain of reasoning**, and the marks are for the links rather than the conclusion. The chain always has the same shape:

**what changed → what that does to the particles → what that does to collisions → what that does to the rate**

Writing *it is faster because it is hotter* skips all three middle steps.

steps.body:
**Part A.**

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Two conditions, not one.** Particles must **collide** *and* the collision must carry at least the **activation energy**. Because most answers remember only the first, the second is where the marks separate — and it is the reason temperature is the most powerful factor.

**Temperature is the only factor that does both.** Concentration, pressure and surface area change the **frequency** of collisions. Temperature changes the frequency **and** the **energy**, so a **greater proportion of collisions exceed the activation energy**. Give one reason for the first three and **two** for temperature, and mark schemes fall into place.

**A catalyst does not push; it opens a shortcut.** It provides an **alternative pathway with a lower activation energy**. It does not give particles energy and it does not make them collide more often. Saying *it lowers the activation energy* is good; saying *it provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy* is the specification's own wording and is what the mark scheme asks for.

**On the profile, only the hump moves.** The **reactants** and **products** stay where they are, so the **overall energy change is unchanged**. A diagram that lowers the product level has drawn a **different reaction**, not a catalysed one — and a claim that a catalyst makes a reaction release more energy is wrong for the same reason.

**Identify a catalyst by its absence.** It speeds the reaction up, it is **unchanged at the end**, and it is **not in the equation**. That last test is the practical one: scan the equation, and if the substance is not there, it was not consumed.

**Rate is not yield.** Every factor in this topic changes **how fast** the product forms, not **how much**. Powdered zinc and granulated zinc of the same mass give the **same volume of hydrogen**; the powder simply gets there sooner. Questions pair these deliberately, and answering *more gas* instead of *the same gas, faster* is the commonest single error in the unit.

**Use proportionality where the question invites it.** Doubling the concentration roughly **doubles** the collision frequency and so roughly **doubles** the rate. The spec asks for *simple ideas about proportionality*, which is exactly this — not an exact calculation, but a defensible estimate.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Reactions occur only when particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.**
- The **activation energy** is the **minimum energy** particles must have to react.
- A collision below the activation energy achieves **nothing**.
- **Concentration, pressure and surface area** increase the **frequency** of collisions.
- **Temperature** increases the **frequency** of collisions **and** makes them **more energetic**.
- So more collisions **exceed the activation energy** at a higher temperature — the half most often left out.
- **Concentration** applies to solutions; **pressure** to gases; **surface area** to solids.
- Smaller pieces have a greater **surface area to volume ratio**: halving a 2 cm cube to 1 cm takes it from **3 : 1** to **6 : 1**.
- **Catalysts change the rate but are not used up.**
- **Different reactions need different catalysts**; **enzymes** are biological catalysts.
- **A catalyst provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy.**
- On a reaction profile the **hump is smaller** but the **reactant and product levels are unchanged**.
- So the **overall energy change is the same** with or without a catalyst.
- Identify a catalyst because it **speeds up the reaction**, is **unchanged at the end**, and is **not in the equation**.
- Every factor here changes the **rate**, not the **amount** of product.
- **Simple proportionality**: doubling the concentration roughly doubles the rate.

questions.prompt: Use collision theory to explain why increasing the temperature, the concentration and the surface area all increase the rate of a reaction, and explain why temperature has the largest effect.
questions.solution:
**Collision theory** says that a reaction can happen only when reacting particles **collide with each other** and do so **with sufficient energy**. The minimum energy needed is the **activation energy**; a collision carrying less than that achieves nothing, and the particles simply bounce apart. It follows that a reaction can be speeded up in two ways: by making collisions **more frequent**, or by making a **greater proportion of them energetic enough**.

**Increasing the concentration** of a solution puts **more particles into the same volume**. They are therefore **closer together** and **collide more often**, so the rate increases. Roughly doubling the concentration roughly doubles the collision frequency, and so roughly doubles the rate.

**Increasing the surface area** — by breaking a solid into smaller pieces or grinding it to a powder — **exposes more of the solid**, so **more of its particles are available to be collided with**. The **surface area to volume ratio** rises: halving a 2 cm cube to 1 cm takes it from **3 : 1** to **6 : 1**. Again the collisions become **more frequent**. Note that the **mass is unchanged**, so the same total amount of product is formed — only sooner.

**Increasing the temperature** is different, and this is the important point. Particles at a higher temperature have **more kinetic energy** and so **move faster**. This has **two** consequences. First, they **collide more frequently**, exactly as with the other factors. Second — and this is the half most often left out — the collisions are **more energetic**, so a **greater proportion of them carry more than the activation energy** and therefore actually result in a reaction.

That second effect is why **temperature has the largest influence**. Concentration, pressure and surface area increase only **how often** particles meet; they do nothing about the fact that most collisions are still too gentle to react. Temperature attacks both limitations at once, which is why a modest rise in temperature can produce a disproportionately large increase in rate.

It is worth being precise about what temperature does **not** do: it does **not lower the activation energy**. The barrier stays exactly where it is — more particles simply have enough energy to get over it. Lowering the barrier itself is what a **catalyst** does, by providing a different pathway.

questions.prompt: Explain what a catalyst is, how it increases the rate of a reaction, and what a reaction profile shows about a catalysed reaction compared with an uncatalysed one.
questions.solution:
A **catalyst** is a substance that **changes the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up** during it. At the end of the reaction it is still present, chemically unchanged, and can be recovered and used again. **Different reactions need different catalysts** — there is no universal one — and in living systems the same role is played by **enzymes**, which are biological catalysts.

A catalyst increases the rate by **providing a different pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy**. That phrasing matters, because it rules out the two things people usually assume. A catalyst does **not** give the particles more energy, and it does **not** make them collide more often. It offers an **alternative route** to exactly the same products, and that route has a **lower barrier**.

The consequence follows from collision theory. Reactions happen only when particles collide with at least the **activation energy**. If the activation energy is **lowered**, then a **greater proportion of the collisions that are already happening** now carry enough energy to react. Nothing about the collisions themselves has changed — the same number occur, with the same spread of energies — but more of them are now successful, so the **rate increases**.

On a **reaction profile**, this shows very clearly and very specifically. The **hump is lower**: the peak between reactants and products is reduced, because the activation energy has fallen. But the **reactant level and the product level are exactly where they were**, because the catalyst has not changed which substances are involved or how much energy they contain.

That has an important consequence: the **overall energy change of the reaction is unchanged**. A catalyst cannot make an exothermic reaction release more energy, and it cannot turn an exothermic reaction into an endothermic one. It changes **how quickly** the energy is released, not **how much**. A diagram that lowers the product level along with the hump has drawn a **different reaction**, not a catalysed one.

Finally, a catalyst can be identified from the information in front of you rather than from chemical knowledge: it **increases the rate**, it is **still present unchanged at the end**, and because it is not consumed it **does not appear in the chemical equation** — which is usually the quickest test of the three.

criteria.text: States that a catalyst changes the rate but is not used up, and that different reactions need different catalysts.
Explains that it provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy.
Explains that a lower activation energy means a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react.
States that on the reaction profile only the hump is lowered, and the overall energy change is unchanged.

questions.modelAnswer:
A **catalyst** is a substance that **changes the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up** during it. At the end of the reaction it is still present, chemically unchanged, and can be recovered and used again. **Different reactions need different catalysts** — there is no universal one — and in living systems the same role is played by **enzymes**, which are biological catalysts.

A catalyst increases the rate by **providing a different pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy**. That phrasing matters, because it rules out the two things people usually assume. A catalyst does **not** give the particles more energy, and it does **not** make them collide more often. It offers an **alternative route** to exactly the same products, and that route has a **lower barrier**.

The consequence follows from collision theory. Reactions happen only when particles collide with at least the **activation energy**. If the activation energy is **lowered**, then a **greater proportion of the collisions that are already happening** now carry enough energy to react. Nothing about the collisions themselves has changed — the same number occur, with the same spread of energies — but more of them are now successful, so the **rate increases**.

On a **reaction profile**, this shows very clearly and very specifically. The **hump is lower**: the peak between reactants and products is reduced, because the activation energy has fallen. But the **reactant level and the product level are exactly where they were**, because the catalyst has not changed which substances are involved or how much energy they contain.

That has an important consequence: the **overall energy change of the reaction is unchanged**. A catalyst cannot make an exothermic reaction release more energy, and it cannot turn an exothermic reaction into an endothermic one. It changes **how quickly** the energy is released, not **how much**. A diagram that lowers the product level along with the hump has drawn a **different reaction**, not a catalysed one.

Finally, a catalyst can be identified from the information in front of you rather than from chemical knowledge: it **increases the rate**, it is **still present unchanged at the end**, and because it is not consumed it **does not appear in the chemical equation** — which is usually the quickest test of the three.

examTechnique.body:
Almost every question here is answered with the same chain: **what changed → what that does to the particles → what that does to the collisions → what that does to the rate**. Marks are given for the links, so write them.

The single most valuable habit is remembering that **temperature does two things** and everything else does one. The second most valuable is keeping **rate** and **amount** apart.
examinerErrors: Explaining a temperature rise with **collision frequency only**, and omitting that more collisions **exceed the activation energy**.
Saying a catalyst **gives particles more energy**, rather than providing a **lower-energy pathway**.
Drawing a catalysed profile with the **product level moved**, which changes the overall energy change.
Claiming a catalyst makes a reaction **release more energy**.
Saying a faster reaction produces **more product**, when it produces the same amount sooner.
Giving only the **collision** and not the **sufficient energy** in a statement of collision theory.
Saying that temperature **lowers the activation energy** — that is a catalyst.
Offering **pressure** for a reaction with no gaseous reactants.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer states **both** conditions for a reaction and then uses the second one deliberately: temperature is the strongest factor precisely because it raises the **proportion of collisions above the activation energy**, which the other factors cannot touch. It quotes the specification's own description of a catalyst — **a different pathway with a lower activation energy** — and knows exactly what that implies on a profile: the **hump falls, the ends do not**, so the **overall energy change is unchanged**. It keeps **rate** and **amount** separate, so powder and lumps of equal mass give the **same gas, faster**. And it can identify a catalyst from an equation it has never seen, by noticing what is **missing** from it.
